questions.title: Phosphate group attaches to the 5' carbon of the pentose sugar
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Genetics > Molecular Genetics > Nucleotide Structure
questions.question: In a standard nucleotide, the phosphate group is covalently joined to which specific carbon of the pentose sugar?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbon 2 of the pentose sugar (in deoxyribose) simply lacks a hydroxyl group compared with ribose; it is not the attachment site for the phosphate group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carbon 3 carries the free hydroxyl group that a neighbouring nucleotide's 5' phosphate links to during polymerization; it is not itself the phosphate's attachment site on the same nucleotide.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carbon 4 is part of the sugar ring structure and helps position the 5' carbon exocyclically, but the phosphate group attaches at carbon 5, not carbon 4.
explanations.D: Correct. The phosphate group of a nucleotide is attached to the 5' carbon of the pentose sugar, and this 5'-phosphate is what forms the phosphodiester bond linking one nucleotide to the 3'-hydroxyl of the next, giving the nucleic acid strand its 5'-to-3' directionality. This 5' phosphate is also the reason a nucleic acid strand has an inherent 5'-to-3' directionality, running from a free 5' phosphate end to a free 3' hydroxyl end.

questions.learning_objective: State that the phosphate group of a nucleotide is attached to the 5' carbon of the pentose sugar, and that this 5' phosphate is what links successive nucleotides via a phosphodiester bond to the 3' hydroxyl of the next sugar.
